result: Three KCNMA1 patient variants (N999S, D434G, H444Q) were characterized in heterologous cells using patch-clamp electrophysiology. N999S and D434G showed gain-of-function (GOF) properties with hyperpolarizing shifts in voltage dependence (V1/2: N999S 41±3 mV, D434G 88±2 mV vs WT 125±2 mV), faster activation, and slower deactivation. H444Q showed loss-of-function (LOF) properties with depolarizing shift (V1/2: 155±4 mV), slower activation, and faster deactivation. The relative channel activity ranking was N999S > D434G > WT > H444Q.
evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C33-C45 provide comprehensive electrophysiological characterization with quantitative measurements of V1/2, activation/deactivation kinetics from patch-clamp recordings in HEK293 cells (Figure 1). The data consistently support GOF properties for N999S and D434G, LOF properties for H444Q, and establish a clear functional hierarchy. Statistical comparisons and sample sizes are provided (n=9-12 patches per variant).

result: BK currents in dentate granule neurons were increased in Kcnma1N999S/WT (69% increase, 22.0±1.8 pA/pF) and Kcnma1D434G/WT (73% increase, 20.9±3.2 pA/pF) mice compared to WT littermates (13.0±2.0 and 12.1±2.6 pA/pF respectively). Homozygous Kcnma1D434G/D434G showed the largest increase (203%, 36.7±5.9 pA/pF). Kcnma1H444Q/WT neurons showed no significant differences from WT. This establishes an allelic series: Kcnma1D434G/D434G >> Kcnma1D434G/WT ≈ Kcnma1N999S/WT > Kcnma1H444Q/WT.
evaluation: Claims C7, C10, C13, C61-C65 are supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from dentate granule neurons (Figure 2) with appropriate statistical analysis (two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc). Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-27 neurons from 1-5 mice per genotype). The data show clear genotype-dependent effects consistent with the heterologous cell findings.

result: Action potential firing was increased in Kcnma1N999S/WT neurons (25-30% higher at 160-240 pA, 125% higher maximal firing) and Kcnma1D434G/WT neurons (18-67% higher at 260-400 pA, 113% higher maximal firing) compared to WT littermates. Kcnma1D434G/D434G showed increased firing at 40-220 pA with 117% higher maximal rate. Kcnma1H444Q/WT and Kcnma1H444Q/H444Q showed no differences. The increased firing in GOF variants was associated with faster AHP decay rates, without changes in resting membrane potential or input resistance.
evaluation: Claims C8, C11, C14, C66-C75 are supported by current-clamp recordings from dentate granule neurons (Figure 3) with appropriate statistical analysis. The data show genotype-specific alterations in firing patterns consistent with BK current changes. Action potential waveform analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) provides mechanistic insight linking faster AHP decay to increased firing. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-27 neurons).

result: Seizure thresholds were decreased in Kcnma1N999S/WT mice (latency to first seizure: 75±15 s vs WT 294±99 s) and Kcnma1D434G/WT mice (101±27 s vs WT 209±35 s) following PTZ injection. Kcnma1H444Q/WT and Kcnma1−/− mice showed no differences in seizure latency or EEG power compared to WT controls. No spontaneous seizures or interictal epileptiform discharges were observed during 24-hour baseline EEG recordings in any genotype.
evaluation: Claims C9, C12, C15, C76-C82 are supported by PTZ-induced seizure assays with EEG/EMG recordings (Figure 4). Statistical analysis shows significant differences for GOF variants (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.01) but not LOF variants. The absence of spontaneous seizures is appropriately documented. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-18 mice per genotype). The results establish increased seizure susceptibility for GOF but not LOF variants.

result: Kcnma1N999S/WT mice exhibited stress-induced immobility (120±12 s after restraint vs WT 51±10 s) in a novel behavioral assay for paroxysmal dyskinesia. This immobility was abrogated by acute dextroamphetamine treatment (0.5 mg/kg), reducing immobility 3-fold and eliminating the difference from WT littermates. D-amp administration without restraint stress had no effect on immobility, wheel running, or grooming behavior in either genotype.
evaluation: Claims C16, C17, C84-C92 are supported by the restraint stress-induced immobility assay (Figure 5) with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The d-amp rescue experiment demonstrates pharmacological reversal consistent with patient responses. Control experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) rule out baseline effects of d-amp on locomotion or stress response. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-11 mice per group). Automated analysis by a blinded experimenter corroborates manual scoring.

result: Homozygous Kcnma1D434G/D434G mice showed stress-induced immobility (101±11 s) similar to Kcnma1N999S/WT mice, while heterozygous Kcnma1D434G/WT mice had immobility (53±9 s) comparable to WT littermates (63±6 s). This demonstrates a gene dosage effect for the D434G variant in producing PNKD-like behavior.
evaluation: Claims C18, C93-C94 are supported by the restraint stress assay data (Figure 5D) showing that homozygosity is required for D434G to produce PNKD-like immobility. Statistical analysis confirms significant differences (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05). This establishes D434G as less pathogenic than N999S, requiring two copies to manifest the phenotype. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-18 mice).

result: Homozygous Kcnma1H444Q/H444Q mice displayed hyperkinetic behavior after stress with reduced immobility (16±6 s) compared to heterozygous Kcnma1H444Q/WT mice. Similarly, Kcnma1−/− mice showed reduced immobility (27±7 s) with three mice exhibiting hyperactive circling and rapid limb movements. This contrasts with the hypokinetic response of GOF variants.
evaluation: Claims C19, C95-C97 are supported by the restraint stress assay data (Figure 5E-F) showing opposite behavioral responses for LOF variants compared to GOF variants. Statistical analysis confirms significant differences (t-test, p<0.01). The qualitative observations of hyperkinetic behavior provide additional phenotypic characterization. Sample sizes are adequate (n=8-11 mice per genotype).

result: The relative pathogenic potential of patient alleles was established as N999S > D434G > H444Q based on channel properties, neuronal activity, seizure susceptibility, and behavioral phenotypes. Kcnma1N999S/WT mice are validated as a model for PNKD3 with increased seizure propensity. The lethality of homozygous Kcnma1N999S/N999S genotypes underscores the severity of this variant. D434G required homozygosity for PNKD-like immobility. H444Q showed limited pathogenicity with distinct hyperkinetic responses in homozygotes.
evaluation: Claims C20-C21, C102-C108 represent integrative conclusions supported by the combined data from all experimental approaches (Figures 1-6). The pathogenicity ranking is consistently supported across multiple phenotypic measures. The validation of Kcnma1N999S/WT as a PNKD3 model is justified by stress-induced immobility and d-amp responsiveness matching patient phenotypes. The breeding data (C55) supports the lethality inference for homozygous N999S.

result: Kcnma1N999S/WT, Kcnma1D434G/WT, and Kcnma1H444Q/WT mice were grossly normal with no spontaneous paroxysms, gait abnormalities, or seizures during home cage observation. Kcnma1D434G/WT and Kcnma1H444Q/WT intercrosses produced viable homozygous progeny, but Kcnma1N999S/WT intercrosses produced no homozygous pups (0/56 pups from heterozygous crosses), similar to other strong GOF BK mutations showing homozygous lethality.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by breeding records and behavioral observations. The absence of homozygous N999S progeny from multiple breeding attempts (n=10 breedings, 56 pups genotyped) provides strong evidence for lethality. The comparison to Tg-BKR207Q mice (C56) is appropriately cited. The lack of overt spontaneous phenotypes is important for establishing that behavioral phenotypes require specific triggers.

result: Gene expression analysis of hippocampus and cerebellum from Kcnma1N999S/WT mice showed no significant differences in Kcnma1 (1.07-fold, p=0.79) or BKβ subunit expression (Kcnmb1, Kcnmb2, Kcnmb4) compared to WT littermates. This indicates that increased BK currents in N999S neurons result from altered channel properties rather than increased expression.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by microarray data (Mouse Clariom D Assay) with appropriate statistical analysis (ANOVA with eBayes test, FDR correction). Sample size is adequate (n=3 mice per genotype and tissue). The conclusion that functional changes rather than expression changes underlie the phenotype is reasonable, though the microarray cannot distinguish WT from N999S transcripts.

result: Kcnma1N999S/WT mice covered shorter distances in voluntary wheel running compared to WT littermates, not due to decreased maximum speed but increased gaps in activity. These mice also showed decreased time to fall in rotarod and hanging wire assays, suggesting baseline motor coordination deficits or muscle weakness that could contribute to reduced running distance.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are supported by wheel running, rotarod, and hanging wire assay data (Figure 6). Statistical analysis shows significant differences (t-test and repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.05). The interpretation appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about whether reduced running distance reflects PNKD-like episodes or baseline motor deficits. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-12 mice per genotype).

result: Neither lisdexamfetamine (155 ng/ml) nor dextroamphetamine (155 ng/ml) directly affected BK current levels in HEK293 cells expressing BKWT or BKN999S channels (p>0.15). The BK channel inhibitor paxilline (100 nM) fully abrogated currents as a positive control (p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by patch-clamp recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA). The negative result for d-amp/lisdexamfetamine effects on BK currents is important for ruling out direct channel modulation as the mechanism of therapeutic action. Paxilline control validates the experimental approach. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-7 patches).

result: Background information establishes that KCNMA1 encodes BK channels activated by voltage and Ca2+, prominent in CNS and smooth muscle, regulating action potential repolarization, fAHP, firing rates, and neurotransmission. Kcnma1−/− mice show smooth muscle, neurobehavioral, and locomotor deficits but do not overtly exhibit KCNMA1-linked channelopathy symptoms. The largest patient cohort harbors GOF rather than LOF alleles. Structural information locates H444Q and D434G in the AC domain (RCK1) and N999S in the S10 domain (RCK2).
evaluation: Claims C1, C22-C32 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations and structural data (Figure 1A-B, PDB 6V38). These provide essential context for interpreting the experimental results. The structural locations of variants are accurately described and illustrated.

result: Prior patient data establishes that heterozygous KCNMA1 variants are associated with PNKD3 (with or without epilepsy). N999S is the most common de novo variant (~17% of patients), found heterozygous in all cases, with ~50% diagnosed with seizure, PNKD, or both. D434G co-segregates with PNKD and epilepsy in a multi-generation pedigree and is corroborated by animal models. H444Q is found in a single case with additional genetic findings. PNKD3 manifests as postural lapses with immobility occurring hundreds of times per day. D-amp and lisdexamfetamine treat PNKD episodes in patients with N999S and other GOF variants. KCNMA1-linked channelopathy encompasses diverse neurological symptoms, with >40 variants identified, most arising de novo.
evaluation: Claims C2, C46-C52, C83, C111-C124 represent prior knowledge from patient studies supported by appropriate citations. These establish the clinical context and rationale for the mouse model studies. The patient phenotype descriptions are consistent with published literature and provide the basis for validating the mouse models.
